We are now in the #Zettabyte era - generating volumes of data never seen before in human history. With just one zettabyte equivalent to a trillion gigabytes, we often hear data being called the the new oil, gold, or currency. But data only creates value when it is translated into decisions. 

Data centres already consume 1.5–2% of global electricity, rising to 5–20% in major digital hubs, while putting growing pressure on power systems, water, and land. 

At the same time, when the just energy transition and the digital revolution are planned together, clean power and data reinforce each other. When clean energy is combined with digital tools, data, and market intelligence, it becomes a platform for jobs, livelihoods, and sustainable development — not just electrons.

This is why, at UNDP , we are working closely with governments and energy partners to turn data into a development asset for the AI and energy transition. Earlier today, at #WFES2026 we reflected on what we are learning in practice. 
Three strategic insights stand out:

1️⃣Data, digital and AI are now a core asset for clean energy investment and delivery. High-quality energy data can de-risk projects and attract capital — but only if digital energy systems are cyber-secure. As grids become digital, cybersecurity becomes energy security, protecting hospitals, water systems, and local businesses. Geospatial and context-specific data can significantly improve energy planning, identify viable investments, and accelerate rollout.

2️⃣ Focus must shift from data systems to data ecosystems. Energy solutions increasingly generate data, but transformational impact depends on how these data flow across institutions, sectors and stakeholders. Building inclusive energy ecosystems requires systems-level approaches; linking data, energy priorities and development objectives, from national policy to local delivery.	

3️⃣ Data transparency and accountability can make energy systems inclusive. Our data shows 447 million “electrified” people do not actually use power. When energy data is transparent and well-governed, utilities and investors become accountable for who is served and who is left behind — turning energy systems into platforms for livelihoods and inclusive development, not just grid connections.

As we move deeper into the AI and energy transition, the real challenge is not generating more data - but using it effectively and governing it better, together. The future of the energy transition will be shaped not by how much data we generate, but on whether data systems reflect lived realities, enable better decisions, and align digital innovation with equitable energy outcomes
